title: Sworn Translation in Spain: What a Traductor Jurado Is and When You Need It
description: What a sworn translation is in Spain, when officials demand one, why foreign certified translations get rejected, and what it typically costs.
excerpt: Spanish offices will not accept just any translation. Here is what a sworn translator does, when you need one, and how to avoid a rejected application.
tldr: A sworn translation is done, signed and stamped by a translator registered with Spain's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. If a foreign document is going to a Spanish official body, you almost always need one, and a translation certified in another country is usually rejected.

segments.text: "Sworn translation vs certified translation" is one of the most common questions from people dealing with Spanish paperwork, usually just after an application has bounced. The difference matters, because getting it wrong costs you weeks. Here is what a sworn translation actually is, when you need one and how to get the right thing the first time.

A sworn translation (traducción jurada) is made by a traductor jurado, a translator officially appointed by Spain's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. They sign and stamp the translation and certify that it is complete and accurate. That certification is what gives it legal value with Spanish authorities, courts, consulates and notaries.

The important point is who is allowed to do it. Only translators appointed by the Spanish ministry can produce a sworn translation for Spanish purposes. A translation agency abroad, or a notary in your home country, cannot substitute for that unless it actually uses a translator on the Spanish list.

The rule of thumb from official-facing guides is simple: if a document is not in Spanish (or Catalan in Catalonia, where it can be accepted in some contexts) and you are handing it to a Spanish official body, expect to need a sworn translation. Typical cases include:

items: Visa and residency applications, including the digital nomad and non-lucrative routes
Marriage, birth and divorce certificates for civil registry or family matters
Degrees and academic transcripts for study or professional recognition

content.text: Why foreign certified translations get rejected

segments.text: This is the trap. A translation certified by a notary or translator in your home country feels official, and in many countries it is. In Spain it is almost always not enough for immigration and similar procedures. Guides describe the usual result: the office sends a formal request for more documents, and your application stalls while you redo the translation properly.

Some documents also need an apostille or legalisation before they are translated, depending on the country they came from. The order matters, so ask the office that will receive the document exactly what they require before you spend money.

content.text: What it costs and how long it takes

segments.text: Prices vary by translator, language pair and length, and are often charged per page, per word or per document with a minimum. As rough 2026 guidance from published guides, simple certificates such as birth, marriage or criminal-record documents are often quoted from around €40 to €65, with turnaround of a few working days. Longer documents such as academic transcripts can run well over €100, and a few guides quote higher per-page rates. Treat these as ballparks and always ask for a written quote.
Urgent jobs usually cost more, so build translation time into your timeline. Deadlines for visas and residency renewals rarely move.

Ask what you will actually receive. Some translators deliver a signed and stamped paper copy by post, others a digitally signed PDF, and some offer both. Not every office accepts digital copies, so check first, and allow for postage time if you need the original.

content.text: How to choose a sworn translator

items: Ask for their official appointment and check it against the Ministry of Foreign Affairs list of sworn translators
Confirm they translate your exact language pair, because appointments are language specific
Ask whether the price is per page or per document, and whether stamps and delivery are included
Ask if you will receive a signed paper copy, a digitally signed copy, or both, and check which the receiving office accepts
Send the receiving office's requirements to the translator so the formatting matches

faqs.q: What is the difference between sworn and certified translation in Spain?
faqs.a: A sworn translation is made and stamped by a translator appointed by Spain's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and has legal value with Spanish authorities. A certified translation from another country is usually not accepted for Spanish official procedures.

faqs.q: Who can do a sworn translation in Spain?
faqs.a: Only a traductor jurado appointed by the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, for the language pair they are appointed for.

faqs.q: How much does a sworn translation cost in Spain?
faqs.a: Simple certificates are often quoted from around €40 to €65, while longer documents such as transcripts can cost well over €100. Always get a written quote.

faqs.q: Do I need a sworn translation for a Spanish visa?
faqs.a: If any supporting document is not in Spanish, you will usually need a sworn translation of it. Check the exact requirements of the consulate or office that will receive it.

faqs.q: Do I need an apostille as well?
faqs.a: Some foreign documents need an apostille or legalisation before translation. Ask the receiving office, because the requirement depends on the document and the country it came from.
